methodology.title: 2.1 Core Principle: Problem and Solution
content: Problem: Students struggle to use multiple irregular verbs seamlessly in a continuous narrative, often switching back to the present tense or defaulting to regular "-ed" endings when cognitive load increases.

Solution: Guide students through retelling a classic fable ("The Lion and the Mouse") across three sessions. By anchoring the verbs to the Beginning, Middle, and End of a highly familiar and emotional story, students practice mixed irregular verbs in a natural, cohesive context.

methodology.title: 2.2 Session Flow (120 Minutes)
content: Teacher pull-out rotation during independent time:
S1: vocabulary drill — teacher says Vietnamese/mime, student says English + makes sentence.
S2: grammar pattern practice — teacher asks "What did the lion/mouse do?" → student answers using irregular verbs.
S3: VC script rehearsal — student reads aloud, teacher provides pronunciation feedback.

methodology.title: 2.4 Teacher Notes: Pull-Out Tasks & Communicative Task
content: Pull-out oral tasks (teacher does these with 1–2 students while class works):
S1 pull-out: Show flashcard of base verb ("catch") → student says past form ("caught"), meaning, and 1 sentence.
S2 pull-out: Give a story prompt ("The lion was in the net"). Student responds using key verbs ("He felt scared and roared loudly").
S3 pull-out: Assess VC script fluency. Check for overgeneralization errors like "catched" or "waked".

Communicative task (Step 5 — 10 min — MUST have real information gap): Students work in pairs to piece together missing parts of the fable. Materials needed: Print 2 copies of Card A and 2 copies of Card B per pair (Section 8). Step-by-step:
Give Card A to Student A, Card B to Student B. Ensure they hide their cards.
Students ask the provided questions to complete the missing story events.
Students produce: A fully ordered sequence of the fable's events.
woke: Close eyes, then snap them open and stretch.
caught: Clap hands together quickly like a trap shutting.
lion: Make claw hands and pretend to roar.
net: Cross fingers together like a grid.

content: Science: Big Animals and Small Animals

listening_script.text: Once upon a time, there was a big lion and a tiny mouse. One day, the mouse ran across the lion's paw. The lion woke up. He was angry! "I will eat you!" said the lion. "Please don't!" said the mouse. "One day, I will help you!" The lion laughed. But he let the mouse go. A few days later, hunters came to the forest. They caught the lion in a net! The lion roared loudly. He felt scared. The tiny mouse heard the lion. "I will help you!" said the mouse. The mouse chewed the net. The lion was free! "Thank you, little friend!" said the lion. "You helped me!" The lion learned: Even small friends can help in big ways.

Science: Symbiosis (Helping Each Other)
[ALL] Read this: In the wild, different animals sometimes help each other. This is a special relationship called "symbiosis" or mutualism. For example, a small bird cleans the teeth of a big crocodile! The bird gets yummy food, and the crocodile gets clean teeth without going to the dentist. In our story, the mouse and the lion helped each other. When two different animals work together, they both survive and win!
